iq-as-01.answer: The OWASP Top 10 is the consensus list of the most critical web application security risks, refreshed roughly every 3-4 years. The current 2021 edition covers Broken Access Control (A01), Cryptographic Failures (A02), Injection (A03), Insecure Design (A04), Security Misconfiguration (A05), Vulnerable and Outdated Components (A06), Identification and Authentication Failures (A07), Software and Data Integrity Failures (A08), Security Logging and Monitoring Failures (A09), and SSRF (A10). I'd pick Broken Access Control and Injection. For Broken Access Control I test by enumerating user roles, then manipulating IDs in URLs and request bodies to access another user's data, plus forced browsing to admin endpoints. For Injection I focus on SQL injection through Burp's intruder with payloads from PortSwigger's cheat sheet, watching for error-based, boolean-based blind, and time-based responses; I also test stored injections in user-controlled fields rendered server-side.
key_points: Top 10 = consensus list, 2021 edition is current
A01 Broken Access Control moved to #1 in 2021
Test BAC: enum roles, IDOR, forced browsing
Test injection: Burp Intruder, error/blind/time variants

iq-as-02.answer: Reflected XSS is when user input is echoed back in the same response without proper encoding — typically through a search box or error message. Stored XSS is when the payload is persisted server-side (in a database, log, profile field) and rendered later to any user who views that content. DOM-based XSS happens entirely client-side: JavaScript reads from a sink like location.hash and writes it into the DOM via innerHTML or document.write without sanitisation. To test reflected, I inject canary strings like xss1234 into every parameter and check responses for unescaped reflection, then escalate to
key_points: Reflected: same request echoed back
Stored: persists and triggers on other users
DOM-based: pure client-side via JS sinks
Test with canaries, then escalate payload, check rendered context

iq-as-03.answer: The defence-in-depth answer is: use parameterised queries (prepared statements) as the primary control, layer in input validation by allowlist, use an ORM that defaults to parameterisation, enforce least-privilege DB accounts, and add a WAF as a safety net. Parameterised queries send the SQL template and the user data on separate wire channels — the database treats user input strictly as data, never as code. Stored procedures can also be safe but only if they themselves use parameterisation internally; a stored proc that dynamically concatenates parameters into EXEC statements is just as vulnerable. The common confusion is that stored procs are inherently safe — they're not, the protection comes from the parameterisation pattern, not from the procedure wrapper. I always test SP-only endpoints with the same injection payloads.
key_points: Parameterised queries = data on separate channel
Stored procs only safe if internally parameterised
Add: allowlist input validation, least-privilege DB user, WAF
Test stored procs the same way as direct queries

iq-as-04.answer: CSRF tricks an authenticated user's browser into making a state-changing request to a target site without their intent. The attacker hosts a form or image that auto-submits to the victim site; because the browser includes cookies automatically, the request looks legitimate. I test by removing the CSRF token from a state-changing request and checking if it still succeeds, then by swapping a valid token from a different user's session to test for token-binding flaws, then changing the request method (POST to GET). My recommendations to developers: implement synchroniser tokens scoped to the session, use SameSite=Strict or Lax cookies (Lax blocks cross-site POST by default), require re-authentication for sensitive actions, validate the Origin/Referer header on state-changing endpoints, and never accept state-changing operations over GET.
key_points: Browser auto-attaches cookies = the root cause
Test: remove token, swap token, change method
Mitigate: synchroniser tokens, SameSite cookies, Origin check
Re-auth for sensitive ops
follow_ups: How does CSRF work against APIs that use Bearer tokens?

iq-as-05.answer: SSRF is when the server makes an HTTP request to a URL controlled by the attacker. It's devastating in cloud because the server sits inside a trusted network and can reach internal-only endpoints — most critically, AWS's IMDSv1 metadata service at 169.254.169.254, which returns temporary IAM credentials with no authentication. Exploitation scenario: a PDF generator accepts an image URL from user input. I supply http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/, retrieve the role name, then fetch the credential payload. With those AWS keys I can call AWS APIs from outside, often with permissions that include S3 reads or EC2 actions. Mitigation is layered: enforce IMDSv2 (which requires a PUT with token first), validate URL schemes to allowlist http/https, resolve hostnames yourself and block RFC1918 ranges, and run the calling service in a VPC with strict egress rules.
key_points: SSRF = server makes attacker-controlled request
Cloud impact: IMDS at 169.254.169.254 leaks IAM creds
Mitigate: IMDSv2, URL allowlist, resolve+block RFC1918, egress rules
DNS rebinding can bypass naive allowlists

iq-as-06.answer: I follow a structured methodology aligned with PTES and OWASP WSTG. Phase 1 is pre-engagement: scope definition, rules of engagement, in-scope domains, allowed times, escalation contacts, success criteria. Phase 2 is reconnaissance: passive (Shodan, certificate transparency, archive.org, Google dorks) then active (Nmap, subdomain enumeration with Amass and Subfinder, content discovery with feroxbuster). Phase 3 is mapping: spider the app with Burp, identify roles, build an endpoint inventory, classify trust boundaries. Phase 4 is vulnerability identification: I work through the WSTG checklist by category — auth, session management, input validation, business logic, crypto. Phase 5 is exploitation and impact validation, careful never to destroy data. Phase 6 is reporting: executive summary for leadership, technical detail with reproduction steps, screenshots, severity using CVSS, remediation guidance per finding, and a debrief call with the dev team.
key_points: Aligned with PTES + OWASP WSTG
Stages: pre-engagement, recon, mapping, identification, exploitation, report
Always validate impact before reporting
Two-audience report: exec summary + technical detail

iq-as-07.answer: I anchor on the OWASP API Security Top 10, which differs from the web Top 10 — APIs face their own risk profile. The top five I check first: (1) Broken Object Level Authorisation (BOLA/IDOR) — I enumerate object IDs across user accounts; this is the #1 API risk. (2) Broken Authentication — token replay, missing expiry, weak JWT signing, OAuth flow misuse. (3) Excessive Data Exposure — endpoints return whole DB objects and rely on the client to filter; I check responses for PII or internal fields. (4) Lack of Resources / Rate Limiting — I script abuse patterns to look for missing throttles, especially on auth and search endpoints. (5) Mass Assignment — I add fields like isAdmin or role to JSON bodies to see if they bind. Tooling: Burp for proxying, Postman or curl for crafting, plus the Swagger/OpenAPI spec if exposed.
key_points: OWASP API Top 10 is distinct from web Top 10
Top 5: BOLA, broken auth, excessive data exposure, rate limiting, mass assignment
Always test with the Swagger/OpenAPI spec if available
Object IDs are #1 attack surface in APIs
follow_ups: What's the difference between BOLA and BFLA?

iq-as-08.answer: Authentication is verifying who you are. Authorisation is deciding what you can do once authenticated. Two auth flaws: missing brute-force protection on login (no rate limit, no account lockout, no MFA) which enables credential stuffing; and weak password reset tokens that are predictable or don't expire, letting an attacker take over accounts by guessing or reusing tokens. Two authorisation flaws: IDOR where /api/orders/123 returns any order regardless of who owns it because the server doesn't check ownership; and privilege escalation where a normal user can call an admin endpoint because the server only renders UI conditionally but doesn't enforce role at the API layer. The common pattern: developers conflate the two and assume that if you're logged in, you're allowed. Authorisation must be checked on every request, at the data layer, never trusting the client.
key_points: AuthN = who; AuthZ = what they can do
AuthN flaws: brute force, weak resets
AuthZ flaws: IDOR, missing role check at API layer
Enforce authZ server-side on every request
follow_ups: How do you design authorisation for a multi-tenant SaaS?

iq-as-09.answer: I start with threat modelling the application — what does it do, what's the data, who are the trust boundaries. Then I prioritise by attack surface: auth, session, input handling, file uploads, deserialisation, crypto, and access control checks. I run SAST (Semgrep, SonarQube, CodeQL) to surface low-hanging issues, but I never trust the tool alone — I read the diff and the auth/authz code paths manually. Top things I look for first: hardcoded secrets, weak crypto (MD5, SHA1, ECB mode), missing access control checks at the start of sensitive endpoints, unsafe deserialisation, raw SQL string concatenation, and shell command execution with user input. I prioritise by impact and reachability — a SQL injection in a public endpoint beats one buried behind admin auth. I deliver findings with code line references, proof-of-concept payload, business impact, and a fix snippet.
key_points: Threat model first, then prioritise by attack surface
SAST tools surface issues; manual review confirms
Priority by impact + reachability, not raw count
Always deliver findings with PoC + fix snippet

iq-as-10.answer: IDOR — Insecure Direct Object Reference — is when an application exposes a reference to an internal object (like a database ID or filename) without checking whether the current user is authorised to access that object. Example in e-commerce: a customer views their invoice at GET /invoices/4521 and downloads the PDF. The server fetches invoice 4521 from the database without verifying that user.id == invoice.owner_id. The attacker simply changes the URL to /invoices/4522, /invoices/4523 and downloads every other customer's invoice — full PII, billing addresses, payment last-4s, purchase history. I test by capturing requests in Burp, identifying every ID parameter (URL paths, query strings, JSON body, cookies, hidden fields), then swapping to IDs owned by a second test account. The fix is server-side ownership checks at the data layer, ideally enforced by row-level security or scoped queries (WHERE owner_id = current_user).
key_points: IDOR = missing ownership check on object reference
Common in: invoices, profiles, files, tickets, orders
Test: enum every ID across two accounts
Fix: server-side ownership check, scoped queries

iq-as-11.answer: JWT is a stateless token with three parts — header, payload, signature — base64url encoded and dot-separated. The header declares the signing algorithm, the payload holds claims (sub, exp, iat, custom claims), and the signature ensures integrity. Common vulnerabilities: (1) alg:none — older libraries accept tokens with alg set to none, skipping signature verification entirely; the attacker forges any payload. (2) Weak HMAC secret — short or guessable secrets can be brute-forced offline with hashcat once you have a token; secrets like 'secret' or 'changeme' are common. (3) Algorithm confusion — token signed with RS256 (asymmetric) is verified using the server's public key as if it were an HMAC secret; the attacker forges tokens by signing with that public key as the HMAC key. (4) JWKS injection — if the server fetches signing keys from a URL embedded in the token's jku header without validating the origin, the attacker hosts their own JWKS and points to it.
key_points: 3 parts: header, payload, signature
Top flaws: alg:none, weak HMAC secret, alg confusion, jku/kid injection
Always pin the algorithm server-side, ignore the header's alg claim
Short-lived tokens + refresh pattern reduces blast radius

iq-as-12.answer: XXE — XML External Entity — exploits XML parsers that process external entity references. The attacker submits XML with a DOCTYPE declaration defining an entity that loads an external resource: <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">. When the parser expands the entity, it reads the local file and either reflects it in the response or sends it out-of-band. I test by intercepting any XML-accepting endpoint (SOAP, file upload that parses XML internally like DOCX or SVG, REST endpoints with Content-Type: application/xml) and injecting an external entity targeting /etc/passwd or a Burp Collaborator URL. Worst-case impact is full file disclosure (config files, source code, AWS credentials), SSRF to internal networks, and on older Java parsers, remote code execution via the expect:// protocol. Mitigation is disabling external entity resolution in the parser — libxml2's XML_PARSE_NOENT off, Java's setFeature for disallow-doctype-decl true.
key_points: XXE = external entity expansion in XML
Impact: file disclosure, SSRF, sometimes RCE
Test endpoints: SOAP, SVG/DOCX upload, anything with XML Content-Type
Fix: disable external entities in the parser config

iq-as-13.answer: Threat modelling is the structured process of identifying what could go wrong before code ships. I've primarily used STRIDE because it's broad and developer-friendly. STRIDE walks through six categories — Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege — applied to each component of a system diagram. We'd typically run a 90-minute session per service with engineering, draw the data flow diagram, mark trust boundaries, then walk component-by-component asking STRIDE questions. I've used DREAD historically for scoring risk but it's subjective so most teams have dropped it in favour of CVSS or risk matrices. PASTA is more enterprise-grade — it links threat modelling to business impact and is good for executive buy-in but it's heavier. For an MVP I'd run STRIDE. For a regulated FS product I'd layer PASTA on top.
key_points: STRIDE: Spoofing/Tampering/Repudiation/Info-disclosure/DoS/EoP
DREAD subjective, mostly replaced by CVSS
PASTA links threats to business impact, heavier process
Always start from a data flow diagram + trust boundaries

iq-as-14.answer: SAST is Static Application Security Testing — analyses source code or compiled bytecode without running it, looking for known dangerous patterns. DAST is Dynamic Application Security Testing — exercises the running application from outside, sending HTTP requests and observing responses. SAST catches issues like hardcoded secrets, raw SQL string concatenation, weak crypto, and insecure deserialisation; it sees code DAST never reaches because DAST only finds what it can route to. DAST catches runtime issues SAST misses entirely: server misconfiguration, missing security headers, broken access control in production, TLS issues, and any issue where the vulnerable behaviour only emerges from the interaction of multiple components. Example: SAST flags a SQL string concatenation. DAST finds the same endpoint requires admin auth that's missing — a broken access control vuln that SAST can't see because it's a runtime property.
key_points: SAST = source code analysis, no execution
DAST = black-box runtime testing
SAST: hardcoded secrets, code smells, broad coverage
DAST: runtime config, auth, broken access control

iq-as-15.answer: CVSS gives a baseline, but I always adjust for context. The factors I weigh beyond raw score: reachability (is the vulnerable endpoint reachable from the internet, or only from authenticated internal users?); business criticality of the affected asset (a SQL injection in a CMS dev environment ranks lower than a low-severity issue in the payments path); data sensitivity (does this expose PII, PCI, regulated data?); exploit availability (is there a public PoC or weaponised exploit in the wild?); detective controls in place (will WAF or runtime monitoring catch exploitation?); compensating controls (is the system behind a VPN, IP allowlisted?); and chainability (does this finding combine with another to escalate impact?). I deliver a prioritised list grouped Critical / High / Medium / Low with a clear 'fix these first' top-5, not just a raw CVSS-sorted dump. Vendor reports that just sort by CVSS are useless to remediation teams.
key_points: CVSS is a starting point, not the answer
Adjust for: reachability, asset criticality, data sensitivity
Consider: public exploits, detective controls, chainability
Deliver a top-5 prioritised list, not a CVSS dump

iq-as-16.answer: On a Cubic Telecom engagement I was assessing the API gateway for a telematics platform. While testing the device-provisioning endpoint I noticed the JWT used for inter-service auth was signed with HS256 and the secret had been committed to a public-facing example repo years before. I extracted it, forged a token with elevated service-account claims, and demonstrated I could provision fictitious devices and read telemetry from any vehicle in the fleet — a critical-rated finding with reachable impact to PII and potentially safety-impacting commands. I reported it through the agreed channel: encrypted email to the security contact, a private Slack channel for clarification, and a full write-up with PoC, scope of impact, and remediation steps (rotate the secret, move to asymmetric RS256, bind tokens to source service identity). The fix shipped within 48 hours. I never disclosed externally and the finding remains confidential under NDA.
key_points: Concrete real example, owned context
Showed reasoning + impact + reporting discipline
Mention coordinated disclosure + NDA respect
Demonstrate technical depth without name-dropping victims

iq-as-17.answer: My core stack: Burp Suite Professional as the proxy and engagement workbench — Repeater, Intruder, Collaborator, Logger++ extension, Active Scan++ for additional checks. Browser dev tools and the Wappalyzer extension for tech fingerprinting. Nmap for network discovery. ffuf or feroxbuster for content discovery — faster and lower noise than dirb. Amass and Subfinder for subdomain enumeration. SQLmap for confirmed injection points but never as a first move because it's noisy. Nuclei for templated vulnerability scanning across many subdomains. JWT.io and jwt_tool for token analysis. PortSwigger Web Academy and the OWASP cheat sheets as my reference. For mobile, MobSF, Frida, Objection. For API work, Postman or Insomnia plus the OpenAPI/Swagger spec. I deliberately avoid tools that automate exploitation without consent — they create false-positive noise and can damage targets.

Discovery: Nmap, ffuf, Amass, Subfinder
Templated scanning: Nuclei
Token analysis: jwt_tool; API: Postman + Swagger

iq-as-18.answer: Business logic flaws don't fit a payload — they require understanding what the application is meant to do and then asking 'what if the user does this thing the developer didn't anticipate'. I map the legitimate workflow first (account creation, KYC, deposit, withdrawal, transfer) then look for assumptions that can be violated. Financial example: a money transfer flow that takes amount and destination. The frontend validates amount > 0 but the backend doesn't, and accepts negative amounts. A transfer of -100 from victim to attacker actually credits the attacker and debits the victim — the sign is reversed. I've also seen: cashback applied twice via race condition on a single coupon, FX rate locked in step 1 and a 30-second delay until commit lets attackers wait for favourable rate movement, and refund flows that don't validate the original transaction belongs to the user. These are all worth more than any SQL injection and you only find them by understanding the domain.
key_points: Logic flaws ≠ payloads, require domain understanding
Map workflow, then ask 'what assumption can be broken'
Common patterns: sign reversal, race conditions, refund flows
Real-world impact often higher than tech vulns

iq-as-19.answer: My baseline: Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) with max-age 31536000 and includeSubDomains to force HTTPS across the domain tree. Content-Security-Policy as the main defence-in-depth against XSS and data exfiltration — properly scoped script-src and default-src, no unsafe-inline. X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff to prevent MIME-type confusion. X-Frame-Options: DENY or CSP frame-ancestors 'none' to block clickjacking. Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin to reduce information leakage. Permissions-Policy to disable unused browser features like camera, microphone, geolocation. Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp if you need isolation for Spectre mitigations. I check these with securityheaders.com and Mozilla Observatory and verify they're set at every response, not just on the homepage. Cache-Control with no-store on auth pages prevents back-button credential exposure.
key_points: HSTS, CSP, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy
Permissions-Policy + COOP/COEP for modern hardening
CSP is the highest-effort highest-value control
Verify headers on every response, not just /

iq-as-20.answer: OAuth 2.0 is an authorisation framework — the canonical flow is the authorisation code with PKCE. The user clicks login, the client redirects to the authorisation server with client_id, redirect_uri, scope, state, and a PKCE code_challenge. The user authenticates and consents, the auth server redirects back to the client with a code and state. The client exchanges that code at the token endpoint, sending the code_verifier; the auth server validates the verifier, returns an access token and optionally refresh token. The client uses the access token to call APIs. Common misconfigurations: missing state parameter enables CSRF on the OAuth flow itself; permissive redirect_uri matching (open redirect or partial match) lets attackers steal codes; implicit flow still in use leaking tokens via URL; missing PKCE on public clients; over-broad scopes; long-lived tokens with no rotation; and confusing OAuth (authZ) with OpenID Connect (authN) — using an access token to identify a user is wrong.
key_points: OAuth = authorisation, not authentication
Auth code + PKCE is the modern default
Common bugs: missing state, loose redirect_uri, implicit flow, no PKCE
OpenID Connect sits on top for identity

iq-as-21.answer: Insecure deserialisation is when an application deserialises attacker-controlled data using a format that allows arbitrary object instantiation or method invocation — Java's ObjectInputStream, .NET's BinaryFormatter, Python's pickle, PHP's unserialize, Ruby's Marshal. The attacker crafts a payload that, upon deserialisation, triggers a chain of method calls (a 'gadget chain') culminating in arbitrary code execution. The classic example is ysoserial for Java — it generates payloads that exploit common libraries like commons-collections. I escalate to critical when: (1) the deserialisation endpoint is reachable from the internet without authentication, (2) the application uses an exploitable format with known gadget chains and the runtime has those libraries available, (3) RCE on the server gives lateral movement potential, or (4) the affected service holds sensitive data or has elevated network access. Even without RCE, deserialisation can give denial of service or info disclosure — but RCE is the worst case and it's commonly achievable.
key_points: Dangerous formats: Java OIS, .NET BinaryFormatter, pickle, unserialize
ysoserial generates Java payloads
Critical when: internet-reachable + gadget available + RCE
Mitigate: use JSON not binary serialisation, deny-list classes

iq-as-22.answer: Broken access control means the system fails to enforce that users can only do what they're authorised to do. Three concrete examples across layers: (1) URL/route layer — /admin/users renders the admin panel because the React app hides the link from non-admins, but anyone who guesses the URL gets full admin functionality because the backend doesn't check role. (2) Object/data layer — GET /api/orders/123 returns order 123 to anyone authenticated, ignoring ownership. This is IDOR/BOLA. (3) Function/method layer — the user-facing /api/posts/123 endpoint accepts a PATCH with isPinned:true; only moderators should be able to pin posts, but the field passes through to the database because of mass assignment with no role-based field allowlisting. All three share the same root cause: authorisation logic is missing or only enforced at the UI/edge, not at the data layer where it belongs.
key_points: BAC ranks #1 in OWASP Top 10 2021
Layers: URL/route, object/data, function/field
Mass assignment is a function-layer BAC issue
Always enforce authZ at the data layer

iq-as-23.answer: GraphQL has its own attack surface that REST testing misses. First, I look for introspection — if /graphql responds to a __schema query, I have the full type system and can map every query, mutation, and field. If introspection is disabled, I try common queries or look for source maps. Then I test: (1) authorisation per field — GraphQL frequently has authZ at the resolver level, and developers miss fields on shared types; I query sensitive fields like email or paymentToken directly. (2) Batching attacks — sending many queries in one request bypasses rate limits and can amplify brute force. (3) Query depth and complexity — recursive queries can DoS the server if no depth/cost limit is enforced. (4) Mutations exposing internal admin operations. Difference from REST: there's no URL surface to map — endpoints are queries inside a single POST. Burp and InQL extension or graphw00f are essential. Authorisation must be enforced at the resolver level, not at the endpoint.
key_points: Introspection = full schema disclosure
Test: per-field authZ, batching, depth/complexity, mutations
Tooling: InQL Burp extension, graphw00f
AuthZ must be at resolver level, not endpoint

iq-as-24.answer: A web race condition exists when the application's correctness depends on the order of concurrent requests, and that order isn't enforced atomically at the data layer. Example: a 'redeem coupon' endpoint reads the coupon's usage_count, checks it's less than max_uses, then increments. If I fire 50 redeem requests in parallel, all 50 may read the same usage_count before any increment commits — and all 50 succeed, even though only 1 should. The classic exploitation pattern is the 'single-packet attack' where you batch requests so they arrive in the same TCP frame: Burp's repeater group with parallel mode does this. To exploit: identify any check-then-act operation (refunds, vote, friend-request accept, MFA enrolment), batch-send, observe state. Fix is server-side: use database transactions with row locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE), or atomic operations (UPDATE...SET count=count+1 WHERE count<max returning), or distributed locks for cross-service flows.
key_points: Race condition = order matters but isn't enforced
Single-packet attack = parallel requests in same TCP frame
Common patterns: coupon, MFA enrol, refund, friend accept
Fix: DB transactions with row locks or atomic updates

iq-as-25.answer: I lead with impact, not technique. I avoid jargon and frame the conversation in terms the developer cares about — production users, revenue, regulatory exposure, on-call burden. I'd say something like: 'This SSRF in the avatar upload lets any logged-in user reach our metadata service and pull AWS keys for the application role. With those keys an attacker can read the customer S3 bucket — the same bucket holding the recent leak of patient names that triggered the GDPR audit.' Then I walk them through a live demo of the exploit so it's concrete, not theoretical. If they still push back, I ask what evidence would change their mind and offer to write the regression test myself. I never make it adversarial — the goal is to get the fix shipped, not to win the argument. If we're stuck, I escalate through their lead, framing it as a risk decision that needs an owner — not a security-vs-dev fight.
key_points: Lead with impact in their language, not technique
Live demo of the exploit beats theory
Offer to write the regression test yourself
Escalate as a risk decision, not a fight

How do you keep relationships when you keep finding bugs?

iq-as-26.answer: Subdomain takeover happens when a DNS record (typically CNAME) points at a third-party service that no longer hosts the resource — the attacker registers the orphaned resource on that service and claims the subdomain. Classic targets: a CNAME from blog.example.com pointing to example.azurewebsites.net that's been decommissioned; an attacker creates an Azure web app with the same name and now controls blog.example.com, including the ability to serve cookies under that domain. I automate discovery at scale with: (1) Subfinder/Amass for the full subdomain inventory, (2) dnsx for resolving CNAMEs, (3) nuclei with the subdomain-takeover templates, or subjack/SubOver for targeted checks. The trick is sequencing — enumerate, resolve, check for dangling CNAMEs, then fingerprint the target service for known takeover patterns. I run this nightly on bug bounty targets and weekly on internal asset inventories.
key_points: Dangling CNAME = attacker registers orphaned resource
Targets: Azure, GitHub Pages, S3, Heroku, Fastly, etc.
Pipeline: Subfinder/Amass → dnsx → nuclei/subjack
Impact: cookie domain takeover, phishing under legitimate brand

iq-as-27.answer: I follow the OWASP MASTG — Mobile Application Security Testing Guide — split into static (analyse the binary, decompile, check hardcoded secrets, weak crypto, certificate pinning) and dynamic (intercept traffic, hook runtime, test the API the app calls). My toolkit: MobSF for the first pass static scan, jadx and apktool for Android decompilation, Hopper or Ghidra for iOS, Frida for runtime hooking, Objection as a higher-level Frida wrapper, Burp with a mobile certificate installed for traffic interception. iOS vs Android differences: iOS apps are signed, sandboxed more strictly, and require a jailbroken device for full Frida access — usually I use a corellium VM or a physical jailbroken test device. Android is easier — I can install APKs freely, root with Magisk, and bypass cert pinning with Frida scripts or Objection. The biggest gotcha on iOS is certificate pinning bypasses break with each OS update and require Frida script maintenance.
key_points: MASTG = OWASP mobile testing guide
Toolkit: MobSF, jadx/apktool, Frida, Objection, Burp + mobile cert
iOS: signed, sandboxed, needs jailbreak
Android: rooting, APK install, easier for testing

iq-as-28.answer: First action: stop testing the IDOR and document the finding immediately. I capture the request and response showing successful unauthorised access, screenshot the proof, and note timestamps. Then I contact my point of contact via the agreed channel — not Slack if it's a public channel, but the dedicated security email or encrypted channel from the engagement letter. The message says: critical finding, production data exposure, need to discuss before continuing testing. I don't enumerate other users' records to 'measure scope' — that would expand the breach. I wait for direction; the client may want to immediately patch and validate, or pause my testing while they investigate, or ask me to verify the fix. I follow their lead. I document everything for the final report including: the request, the redacted response, severity rationale, recommended fix, and timeline of disclosure. The principle: minimise additional harm, maximise visibility to the right people, defer to the client.
key_points: Stop testing, document, escalate via agreed channel
Don't enumerate scope yourself
Defer to client on next steps
Document for the report with redacted PoC
follow_ups: What if the client asks you to keep testing?
How do you handle a finding that exposes regulated data?

iq-as-29.answer: The OWASP Web Security Testing Guide is the most comprehensive structured methodology for web app pentesting. It organises tests into categories: information gathering, configuration management, identity management, authentication, authorisation, session management, input validation, error handling, cryptography, business logic, and client-side. Each test has a unique ID (e.g., WSTG-AUTH-04) with description, how to test, tools, references. I use it as my engagement checklist — I work through each category and tick off tests applicable to the target. It prevents me from over-indexing on what I'm comfortable with (web app injection) and ensures I cover the unsexy categories (session management, error handling). My workflow: I clone the WSTG markdown locally, create an engagement checklist from it, mark each test status as I go (passed/failed/N/A/skipped with rationale). The final report references WSTG IDs which clients increasingly expect — it shows methodological rigour and gives them a frame they recognise.
key_points: WSTG = OWASP's structured web testing methodology
Categories: info gathering, authN, authZ, session, input, business logic
Use as engagement checklist to prevent bias
Reference WSTG IDs in reports for methodology proof
follow_ups: How does WSTG differ from OSSTMM?
Have you contributed to the WSTG?

iq-as-30.answer: I write two distinct artefacts. For the CISO/leadership: a one-page executive summary with strategic findings — high-level risk picture, top 5 issues by business impact (not technical severity), trend versus previous assessment, and recommended programme-level investments (e.g., 'three of five criticals stem from missing access control enforcement at the data layer — recommend a Q1 architecture review'). No payload screenshots, no jargon. For the dev team: detailed per-finding writeups with reproduction steps, request/response screenshots, affected endpoint, code-level fix recommendation with snippet, CWE reference, regression test suggestion, and remediation verification steps. I structure findings by component so a frontend dev isn't paging through API findings. I include a Q&A section addressing pushback I anticipate. I always offer to walk the report through with the team — written reports get skimmed; live walkthroughs land. The two artefacts share the same data but serve different decisions: invest vs. fix.
key_points: Two artefacts: CISO exec summary, dev technical detail
CISO: strategic, business-impact framed, no jargon
Dev: per-finding, reproduction steps, code-level fixes
Always offer a live walkthrough
follow_ups: Have you ever had a finding disputed by the dev team?
How do you track remediation across cycles?

iq-soc-01.answer: Step 1: receive the alert in the SIEM — phishing email reported by a user or detected by the mail gateway. I open the ticket in the case management system and acknowledge ownership. Step 2: triage — pull the email headers, sender domain, attachments, URLs. Check the sender's SPF/DKIM/DMARC alignment, look up the domain age, run the URL through urlscan.io and the attachment through a sandbox like Joe Sandbox or our internal Cuckoo. Step 3: scope — query the mail gateway for other recipients of the same email, query proxy logs to see if anyone clicked the URL, query EDR for execution of any attachment. Step 4: contain — if anyone clicked or executed, isolate those endpoints via EDR and force password reset for the user account. Step 5: eradicate — remove the email from mailboxes using PowerShell or Microsoft Defender Search-And-Delete, block the sender domain and URL at the gateway and proxy. Step 6: notify the user, document the IOCs, update detection rules. Step 7: close the ticket with a writeup.
key_points: Lifecycle: triage → scope → contain → eradicate → notify → document
Triage: headers, SPF/DKIM/DMARC, sandbox URL+attachment
Scope across mail, proxy, EDR
Always pull the email from other mailboxes
follow_ups: How do you handle a phishing email that targets the CFO?
What detection rules would you add after this incident?

iq-soc-02.answer: NIST 800-61 defines four phases: Preparation, Detection and Analysis, Containment/Eradication/Recovery, and Post-Incident Activity. Preparation: build the IR team, define roles, write playbooks, ensure tooling (SIEM, EDR, forensic tooling, evidence storage) is ready, run tabletop exercises. Detection and Analysis: receive an alert, validate it isn't a false positive, scope the incident, classify severity, assign an incident commander. Containment, Eradication, Recovery: short-term containment isolates the affected systems to stop spread; long-term containment patches and hardens before bringing systems back; eradication removes the threat (malware, attacker accounts, persistence); recovery restores systems to production. Post-Incident: writeup, root cause, lessons learned, IOC sharing, detection rule updates, playbook updates. Example: a ransomware infection — preparation meant we had immutable backups, detection caught lateral movement via EDR, containment isolated the affected segment via network blocks, eradication wiped the boxes, recovery restored from backup, post-incident drove a 12-week project to deploy MFA on RDP.
key_points: NIST 800-61 = 4 phases
Preparation often skipped but is highest leverage
Containment splits into short-term + long-term
Post-incident must drive detection and process improvements
follow_ups: Compare NIST 800-61 to SANS 6-step.
What goes in a tabletop exercise?

iq-soc-03.answer: I weigh: source reliability (the SIEM rule that just fired — how often does it produce true positives historically?), context fit (does the alert pattern match the user's baseline behaviour or known business activity?), corroboration (is there a second telemetry source confirming the activity — EDR, proxy, DNS?), threat intelligence (does the IP, hash, or domain appear in our threat feeds or in recent campaigns?), and asset criticality (a low-confidence alert on a domain controller still gets investigated; the same alert on a sandbox doesn't). I avoid the trap of dismissing alerts just because they're noisy — if a noisy rule fires alongside another signal, the combination shifts probability. My workflow: timestamp, user, asset, source IP, target — gather these in 30 seconds from the SIEM, then 2 minutes of correlation across 2-3 other tools. If I can't confirm true positive within 5 minutes, I escalate or open a deeper investigation rather than close it as FP.
key_points: Source reliability, context fit, corroboration, threat intel, asset criticality
Noisy alerts that combine = real signal
5-minute timebox before escalation or deeper dive
Never close 'noisy' alerts without correlation
follow_ups: How do you track FP rate per rule?
What's the worst false negative you've experienced?

iq-soc-04.answer: MITRE ATT&CK is a knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques, derived from real-world observed behaviours, organised into 14 tactics (Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, Defense Evasion, Credential Access, Discovery, Lateral Movement, Collection, C2, Exfiltration, Impact, Reconnaissance, Resource Development). Each tactic has techniques with IDs (e.g., T1059.001 PowerShell). I've used it three ways: (1) Detection coverage mapping — for each technique relevant to our threat model, do we have a detection? I built a heatmap showing coverage gaps, which drove our detection engineering backlog. (2) Threat hunting — pick a technique like T1003 Credential Dumping, build a hunting hypothesis ('attackers use lsass.exe access to dump credentials'), and write a query against EDR telemetry looking for that behaviour. (3) Incident analysis — map observed attacker behaviour to the matrix to identify the campaign's likely TTPs and predict next moves.
key_points: ATT&CK = TTPs from real-world adversary behaviour
14 tactics, hundreds of techniques
Use for: detection coverage, threat hunting, IR analysis
Heatmap coverage drives detection engineering priorities
follow_ups: What's the difference between ATT&CK and the Cyber Kill Chain?
How do you measure ATT&CK detection coverage?

iq-soc-05.answer: I start with the process metadata in EDR: full path, parent process, command line, user context, integrity level, start time, file hash. Red flags: signed by an unexpected vendor or unsigned, parent is winword.exe or outlook.exe (Office spawning a shell), command line has base64 PowerShell or unusual flags, integrity level is high but the user isn't admin, runs from %TEMP% or %APPDATA%. Next I check the hash against VirusTotal, our threat intel, and historical EDR sightings org-wide — is this the only host? Then network: did the process make network connections, to what IPs/domains, are those domains young, do they appear in proxy or DNS logs from other hosts? Then persistence: registry Run keys, scheduled tasks, services created near the process timestamp. Then memory: dump the process with procdump and run strings or analyse with Volatility for injected code. By this point I either have a benign explanation or enough evidence for containment.
key_points: Process metadata first: parent, cmdline, user, integrity, signature
Hash check: VT, internal threat intel, sightings
Network: connections, domain age, peer-host correlation
Persistence + memory if still suspicious

What is process hollowing and how do you detect it?

iq-soc-06.answer: Ransomware moves fast, so log priorities are: (1) EDR telemetry — process executions especially on affected hosts and the patient zero candidate, file rename/extension change events (the ransomware encrypting), shadow copy deletion (vssadmin), and any attempts to disable AV. (2) Windows Security event logs — 4624 (logon), 4625 (failed logon), 4688 (process creation), 4720 (account created), 4672 (special privileges assigned). (3) Sysmon if deployed — process tree, network connections, file create timestamps. (4) Active Directory logs — Kerberos events to identify lateral movement, DCSync attempts (event 4662). (5) Network logs — SMB connection patterns showing fan-out from patient zero. (6) Firewall and proxy — C2 callback URLs, exfiltration destinations. (7) Email and gateway — was the initial vector a phishing attachment? I'd build a timeline anchored on the patient zero process execution and walk forward and backward 24 hours.
key_points: EDR telemetry first — process tree, file ops, shadow deletion
Sysmon if deployed
Network: SMB fan-out, C2 callback, exfiltration
follow_ups: What is vssadmin delete shadows and why detect it?
How do you preserve evidence on encrypted hosts?

iq-soc-07.answer: EDR — Endpoint Detection and Response — sits on each endpoint as an agent collecting telemetry (process, file, network, registry events), running behavioural detections, and providing response actions (isolate, kill process, run a script). Examples: CrowdStrike, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, SentinelOne. SIEM — Security Information and Event Management — is a central platform that ingests logs from EDR, firewalls, proxies, AD, cloud, applications, and runs correlation rules to surface security alerts. Examples: Splunk, Sentinel, QRadar, Chronicle. SOAR — Security Orchestration, Automation, Response — automates response workflows by integrating with the SIEM, EDR, ticketing, and other tools; runs playbooks that triage, enrich, contain, and notify. Examples: Cortex XSOAR, Splunk SOAR. They stack: EDR is the sensor and response surface for endpoints, SIEM aggregates and correlates across the org, SOAR orchestrates the response. A modern SOC pipeline: EDR generates an alert → SIEM correlates with proxy logs to confirm scope → SOAR opens a ticket, isolates the host, notifies the analyst, who validates and closes.
key_points: EDR: endpoint agent, telemetry + response
SIEM: central log correlation across sources
SOAR: playbook automation across tools
They stack: EDR detects, SIEM correlates, SOAR responds

When would you build vs buy a SOAR?

iq-soc-08.answer: Lateral movement in AD typically uses pass-the-hash, pass-the-ticket, RDP, WMI, PsExec, or remote PowerShell. I hunt with these queries: (1) 4624 logon type 3 (network) or type 10 (RDP) from non-IT user accounts to multiple hosts in a short window — most users don't authenticate across many machines. (2) 4648 explicit credential logons (runas) which suggests credential pivoting. (3) PsExec service installation events (7045) on multiple hosts. (4) Suspicious child processes from svchost.exe — wsmprovhost.exe is WinRM execution, often abused. (5) Kerberos events with unusual encryption types (RC4 vs AES) suggesting Kerberoasting or downgrade attacks. (6) Authentication from one host to many DCs in a short window suggesting BloodHound enumeration. I baseline normal authentication patterns per user and per host then alert on deviations. Tools: SIEM queries on Windows Security + Sysmon, plus Bloodhound's reverse to map likely attack paths.
key_points: Common LM: PtH, PtT, RDP, WMI, PsExec, WinRM
Hunt: 4624 type 3/10, 4648, 7045, wsmprovhost, RC4 Kerberos
Baseline user auth patterns, alert on deviation
BloodHound for attack path discovery
follow_ups: What is Kerberoasting and how do you detect it?
How would you detect Golden Ticket?

iq-soc-09.answer: Threat intelligence feeds are streams of IOCs — IPs, domains, hashes, URLs, YARA rules — sourced from commercial providers (Recorded Future, Mandiant, CrowdStrike), open feeds (AlienVault OTX, abuse.ch, MISP communities), or government CERTs. Operationalising IOCs means making them automatically actionable across detection and prevention surfaces. My approach: (1) ingest feeds into a TIP (threat intel platform) like MISP or OpenCTI, which dedupes and scores confidence. (2) push high-confidence IOCs to detection: SIEM watchlists, EDR custom IOC lists, firewall block lists, proxy block lists, DNS sinkholes. (3) automate aging — IOCs decay; an IP that was malicious last month may be legitimate this month, so I expire after 30-90 days unless re-observed. (4) measure: how many alerts did each feed generate, what's the TP rate, what's the cost per TP. Feeds with poor signal-to-noise get deprioritised. (5) contribute back — share confirmed IOCs from internal incidents into MISP.
key_points: Feeds: commercial, open (OTX, abuse.ch), government CERTs
TIP (MISP, OpenCTI) ingests and scores
Push to: SIEM watchlists, EDR, firewall, proxy, DNS
Always age IOCs and measure feed signal-to-noise
follow_ups: What's the difference between strategic, tactical, and operational threat intel?
How do you handle low-confidence IOCs?

iq-soc-10.answer: Anchor on the trigger — what raised the suspicion? DLP alert, EDR detection, abnormal egress volume, threat intel hit, employee tip. From there: (1) Identify the actor — user account, host, source IP. (2) Determine timeline — when did suspicious activity start, what was happening just before. (3) Inventory potentially exfiltrated data — DLP logs, file access events (4663 on file servers), database query logs, cloud storage download logs. (4) Identify the egress channel — proxy logs for HTTPS POSTs to external destinations, DNS queries for tunnelling, email gateway logs for attachments, USB device events from EDR, cloud storage uploads, instant messaging file shares. (5) Look for staging — files copied to temp directories, archives created (.zip/.rar/.7z), unusual encryption activity. (6) Correlate with user behaviour — was the user on leave? Did they just give notice? Has the account been compromised? (7) Contain — disable user, isolate host, block egress destination. (8) Estimate volume and sensitivity for breach notification scoping.
key_points: Start with the trigger that raised suspicion
Pivot: actor → timeline → data → channel → staging
Egress channels: proxy, DNS, email, USB, cloud, IM
Staging signs: archives, encryption, temp dirs
follow_ups: How do you detect DNS tunnelling exfiltration?
What is data staging and what indicators do you watch?

iq-soc-11.answer: I treat detection tuning as a data problem. For each rule I track: total fires per week, true positive count, false positive count, MTTR, and analyst time spent. A rule with high volume and <5% TP rate is a candidate for tuning or retirement. Tuning approaches: (1) Add context filters — exclude known business processes, scheduled jobs, IT admin activity by user/host whitelist, but always with documentation of why. (2) Raise the threshold — instead of alerting on a single failed login, alert on >20 in 5 minutes. (3) Convert to aggregate detection — multiple weak signals correlated together (failed logon + suspicious process + outbound C2) produce a stronger high-confidence alert. (4) Split a noisy rule into a watch-only feed and a high-confidence subset that pages. (5) Retire rules whose threats are now covered by EDR or other layers. I never tune by silencing without rationale — every suppression gets a documented reason and an expiry date.
key_points: Track per-rule: volume, TP rate, MTTR, analyst time
Tune by: context filters, thresholds, aggregation, splitting
Never silence without documented rationale + expiry
Aggregate weak signals beat single noisy rules

What is detection-as-code?

iq-soc-12.answer: DNS tunnelling encodes data into DNS queries — typically the subdomain portion of A or TXT lookups to a domain controlled by the attacker. The recursive resolver routes the query to the attacker's authoritative name server, which decodes and may respond with further commands encoded in the response. It's popular for C2 and exfil because DNS egress is rarely blocked. Detection in SIEM: (1) High-entropy subdomain strings — legitimate DNS names are pronounceable, tunnelled names look random; compute Shannon entropy per query and alert on outliers. (2) Long subdomain length — legitimate subdomains rarely exceed 30-50 characters; tunnels chunk data into 60+ character labels. (3) High query volume to a single domain from one source — exfil produces hundreds or thousands of queries to the same parent domain. (4) Unusual record types — TXT and NULL records are tunnel favourites. (5) Newly registered domain age. Tools like iodine and dnscat2 have known patterns. I baseline domain query patterns and alert on volume and entropy deviation.
key_points: DNS tunnelling = data in subdomain or TXT records
Detect: high entropy, long labels, high query volume per domain
TXT and NULL records are red flags
Newly registered domains add suspicion
follow_ups: How do you detect DoH used for exfil?
What's the difference between iodine and dnscat2?

iq-soc-13.answer: Pass-the-hash exploits Windows NTLM authentication — instead of cracking a password, the attacker steals the NTLM hash from a compromised host's memory (LSASS process) and reuses it directly against other hosts because NTLM accepts the hash as proof of knowledge of the password. Tools: mimikatz, Impacket's wmiexec/psexec. Detection: (1) 4624 logon type 9 (NewCredentials) or unusual logon patterns where one source connects to many hosts in quick succession. (2) Sysmon event 10 (ProcessAccess) targeting lsass.exe — credential dumping precursor. (3) PtH-specific event signatures: 4624 with explicit IP and unusual workstation field. Prevention: (1) Deploy LSA Protection / Credential Guard on Windows 10+. (2) Restrict NTLM via Group Policy where possible, prefer Kerberos. (3) Tier admin accounts — Tier 0 (domain admins) never log into Tier 1/2 systems; this means the high-value hashes never land on machines that get compromised. (4) Local admin password randomisation via LAPS so stolen local hashes don't pivot. (5) Disable WDigest and cached credentials.
key_points: PtH = reuse stolen NTLM hash, no password crack needed
Detection: 4624 logon types, LSASS access in Sysmon
Prevent: LSA Protection, Credential Guard, tiering, LAPS
Disable WDigest + cached credentials
follow_ups: What's the difference between PtH and pass-the-ticket?
How does Credential Guard work under the hood?

iq-soc-14.answer: Step 1: confirm the breach indicator — pull the source (HIBP, paid feed, dark web monitoring), verify the email matches a corporate account, check the breach metadata (when, what data exposed). Step 2: force password reset on the user account immediately — disable session tokens, revoke active sessions in Azure AD / Okta. Step 3: enforce MFA reset if not already MFA-protected. Step 4: query logs — was the credential used? Sign-in logs in Azure AD for the past 90 days; failed attempts from unusual geolocations; successful logins from suspicious IPs; risky sign-in events. Step 5: check downstream — was the same password reused on other corporate systems? If so, sweep those accounts. Step 6: notify the user with what happened, what we did, and what they need to do (change personal accounts that share the password). Step 7: document IOCs (the breach source, exposed dataset) and update detection. Step 8: review broader exposure — were other employees in the same breach? Run a bulk check.
key_points: Confirm → reset → revoke sessions → MFA enforce
Query sign-in logs for actual use
Sweep for reused passwords on other corp systems
Bulk check for other employees in same breach
follow_ups: What is impossible-travel detection and how would you build it?
How do you respond if MFA was already bypassed?

iq-soc-15.answer: I scan the queue and group by alert type first — 30 of those 50 might be the same noisy detection that should be tuned later. From the unique alerts I prioritise by: (1) Asset criticality — domain controllers, payment systems, customer-facing infrastructure, prod databases first. (2) Threat severity — confirmed malware execution or active exploitation before suspicious patterns. (3) Authentication anomalies — successful unusual sign-ins are higher priority than failed ones because failed login is noise, success is impact. (4) Time decay — older alerts may have evolved into incidents while sitting in queue. (5) Existing context — has this user or host already been flagged in another alert? Cluster related alerts. I aim to clear or assign every alert within the shift, even if just to escalate or properly close as known-noise. I keep a running tally so I can show that during peak load 40% of my time went to false positives and back the case for tuning.
key_points: Group by type first to identify noise clusters
Prioritise: asset criticality, threat severity, success over failure
Cluster related alerts on same user/host
Always close or assign — never just skip
follow_ups: How would you propose to leadership to reduce alert volume?
What's a fair MTTR target for L1 triage?

iq-soc-16.answer: Lockheed Martin's Cyber Kill Chain has 7 phases: Reconnaissance, Weaponisation, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, Command and Control, Actions on Objectives. It's a linear adversary model — disrupt any phase and you defeat the campaign. ATT&CK has 14 tactics that don't enforce a linear order, and includes pre-attack tactics (Reconnaissance, Resource Development) that Kill Chain treats abstractly. Mapping: Kill Chain Recon ≈ ATT&CK Reconnaissance and Resource Development; Weaponisation has no direct ATT&CK tactic because ATT&CK focuses on observable behaviours; Delivery ≈ Initial Access; Exploitation ≈ Execution (sometimes Privilege Escalation); Installation ≈ Persistence; C2 ≈ Command and Control; Actions on Objectives ≈ Collection, Exfiltration, Impact. In practice: Kill Chain is the strategic narrative for executive briefings (each phase has a name leadership understands); ATT&CK is the operational detail for detection engineering and threat hunting. I use Kill Chain to tell the story and ATT&CK to plan the defences.
key_points: Kill Chain: 7 linear phases, strategic narrative
ATT&CK: 14 tactics, observable behaviours, non-linear
Recon→Recon+Resource Dev; Delivery→Initial Access
Use both: Kill Chain for narrative, ATT&CK for engineering
follow_ups: What's the Unified Kill Chain?
Where does the Kill Chain break down as a model?

iq-soc-17.answer: A playbook is a documented step-by-step procedure for handling a specific incident type — phishing, malware infection, credential leak, ransomware, DDoS. It standardises response so any analyst can execute consistent quality, and it reduces decision fatigue during high-pressure incidents. I wrote a phishing-with-attachment playbook for my team. Steps: (1) Acknowledge in ticket, set status investigating. (2) Pull email headers, original message, attachment. (3) Detonate attachment in sandbox, capture verdict and IOCs. (4) Query mail gateway for other recipients. (5) If malicious — query EDR for execution of file hash across the org. (6) Block sender domain, file hash, callback C2 in EGR, EDR, proxy. (7) For users who clicked or executed: isolate host, reset credentials, notify the user. (8) Remove email from mailboxes using Search-And-Delete. (9) Update detection rules with new IOCs. (10) Write incident summary and close. The playbook includes Splunk queries, escalation contacts, decision branches.
key_points: Playbook = standardised IR procedure per incident type
Reduces decision fatigue, ensures consistent quality
Real example: phishing with attachment, 10 steps
Include queries, contacts, decision branches

What goes in a tabletop based on a playbook?

iq-soc-18.answer: Common Windows persistence mechanisms: (1) Registry Run/RunOnce keys — HKCU and HKLM Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, where binaries listed launch at user logon or system boot. (2) Scheduled tasks created via schtasks or PowerShell — useful because they trigger on intervals or events. (3) Services — install a Windows service pointing at a malicious binary; runs at boot with system privileges. (4) Startup folder — drop an LNK or executable in %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup. (5) WMI event subscription — register a permanent WMI consumer that triggers on a system event (boot, user logon). (6) DLL hijacking — drop a malicious DLL in a folder Windows searches before the legitimate location. (7) AppInit_DLLs and AppCertDlls — older but still seen. (8) BITS jobs — abuse Background Intelligent Transfer Service for persistence. (9) Office templates, Outlook rules. (10) Bootkit and UEFI implants for the most advanced. I detect with Sysmon registry, file, and process events plus Autoruns scans on suspect hosts.
key_points: Run keys, scheduled tasks, services, startup folder
Advanced: WMI subscription, DLL hijacking, BITS, Office templates
Detection: Sysmon registry/file/process, Autoruns
Map all to ATT&CK Persistence techniques
follow_ups: What is COM hijacking?
How would you hunt for WMI event subscription persistence?

iq-soc-19.answer: First, escalate to incident commander and notify leadership that scope is undetermined — this changes the response from 'contain and continue' to 'contain broadly while we investigate'. Second, broaden containment: rather than isolate just the confirmed-affected host, segment the network where the host lives, force credential resets for users on that segment, restrict outbound to known-good destinations. Third, expand evidence collection — pull memory and disk images from the affected host, request EDR retrospective queries against the IOCs we have, and engage forensics or external IR if internal capacity is exhausted. Fourth, build a working hypothesis of likely attacker behaviour from what's known and hunt explicitly for evidence against that — assume worst case rather than waiting for it to appear. Fifth, document the unknowns explicitly so leadership understands the risk picture. Sixth, communicate timeline and resource needs honestly. The instinct to keep investigating quietly and hope scope is small is exactly the path that produces the multi-month dwell-time horror stories.
key_points: Escalate immediately when scope is undetermined
Broaden containment beyond confirmed scope
Engage forensics / external IR if needed
Document unknowns explicitly for leadership
follow_ups: When do you bring in external IR?
How do you balance containment with business continuity?

iq-soc-20.answer: I split metrics into operational, detection quality, and outcome categories. Operational: MTTD (mean time to detect from compromise to alert), MTTA (alert to acknowledged), MTTR (acknowledge to resolved), alert volume per analyst, queue depth, on-call burden. Detection quality: TP rate per rule, FP rate, detection coverage mapped to ATT&CK, retro-coverage (could we have detected past breaches?), time to integrate new IOCs into detection. Outcome: incidents per quarter by category, mean dwell time (compromise to containment), incidents where we beat the attacker to the goal, customer-impacting incidents prevented. Process: tabletop exercises run, playbooks updated, threat-hunting hours per week, lessons learned implemented. I avoid vanity metrics like 'alerts processed' that incentivise closing alerts as FP. The best single metric is mean dwell time — it captures whether the SOC is actually preventing impact, not just generating activity. I'd also instrument the cost-per-incident to make the business case for tooling.
key_points: Operational: MTTD, MTTA, MTTR, queue depth
Quality: TP/FP rate, ATT&CK coverage, retro-coverage
Outcome: dwell time, prevented impact, business cost
Avoid vanity 'alerts closed' metrics
follow_ups: How do you measure detection coverage in practice?
What metric would you fire first if you took over a SOC?

iq-cloud-01.answer: The shared responsibility model defines what the cloud provider secures versus what the customer secures. The split shifts by service model. In IaaS (EC2, Compute Engine, Azure VMs): the provider secures the physical infrastructure, hypervisor, and network backbone; the customer secures the operating system, applications, runtime, data, configuration, identity, and network controls in the VPC. In PaaS (App Engine, Lambda, Azure App Service): the provider additionally secures the OS, runtime, and application platform; the customer secures the application code, data, identity, configuration. In SaaS (Office 365, Salesforce): the provider secures almost everything; the customer is responsible for data classification, user access management, configuration of the service, and how third-party integrations are connected. The recurring theme: identity, data, and configuration always belong to the customer. The biggest source of cloud breaches is customers misunderstanding the boundary — most famously, public S3 buckets, where the customer assumed AWS would default to private.
key_points: Provider secures up to a certain layer; customer secures above
IaaS: customer owns OS+up; PaaS: app+config; SaaS: data+IAM
Identity, data, config always customer's
Misunderstanding the boundary causes most cloud breaches

iq-cloud-02.answer: Top 5 S3 misconfigurations I check: (1) Bucket policy or ACL granting public read or write — the canonical breach pattern. Use S3 Block Public Access at account level which overrides bucket policies. (2) Bucket policies allowing 'Principal: *' even with conditions that look restrictive — confused-deputy and overly permissive conditions. (3) Missing default encryption at rest — KMS-managed (SSE-KMS) preferred over SSE-S3 for audit trail. (4) Missing versioning + MFA Delete — without versioning, ransomware can encrypt your objects in place. (5) Missing access logging or CloudTrail data events — if a breach happens, you need to know what was accessed. Other items: cross-account roles with wildcard resources, signed URL expiration too long, presigned URLs in source code, bucket names that follow predictable patterns (companyname-prod-data), and replication misconfigurations that copy public access to disaster recovery regions. I scan with Prowler, ScoutSuite, or in-house tools that check these against benchmarks.
key_points: Public bucket = #1 breach pattern
Use S3 Block Public Access at account level
Encryption + versioning + access logging are minimum baselines
Scan with Prowler/ScoutSuite + CSPM tools

iq-cloud-03.answer: Least privilege means each identity has only the permissions necessary for its function, with nothing extra. At scale this is hard because (a) developers want broad permissions to move fast, (b) the AWS API has thousands of actions, (c) what someone needs evolves over time. My approach: (1) Use AWS IAM Access Analyzer to identify unused permissions on roles and recommend tighter policies based on actual usage in CloudTrail. (2) Use Service Control Policies at the organisation level to set absolute guardrails — no account can ever do X. (3) Issue permissions through groups and roles, never directly to users; users only get console federation. (4) Adopt permissions boundaries to cap maximum privileges. (5) Implement just-in-time access using a tool like AWS IAM Identity Center with session tagging — elevated privileges are granted for the duration of a task, not standing. (6) Tag all resources by team and project; use tag-based policies (e.g., 'can only modify resources tagged team=X'). (7) Quarterly audit unused IAM users, access keys older than 90 days, and roles with admin or wildcard policies.
key_points: Access Analyzer recommends tighter policies from CloudTrail
SCPs = absolute guardrails at org level
Groups + roles + permissions boundaries layered
Just-in-time access > standing elevated privileges

iq-cloud-04.answer: I'd structure around CIS Kubernetes Benchmark and the Kubernetes hardening guide from NSA/CISA. Control plane: restrict API server access (private endpoint, VPC-only, allowed IP CIDR), enable audit logging to a SIEM, use RBAC with least privilege, rotate certs. Workload: enforce Pod Security Standards (baseline or restricted), block privileged containers and hostPath mounts via OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno policies, run containers as non-root with read-only filesystem, drop capabilities. Network: default-deny NetworkPolicy then explicit allow per workload, service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) for mTLS between services, network segmentation per namespace. Secrets: external secret store (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager via External Secrets Operator); never bake secrets into images or ConfigMaps. Images: scan in CI (Trivy, Snyk), use admission control to block vulnerable images, use signed images with Sigstore/cosign. Runtime: deploy Falco or Tetragon for runtime threat detection; alert on shells in containers, privilege escalation, suspicious syscalls. Cluster: keep patched, use managed control plane (EKS, GKE) where possible.
key_points: CIS Kubernetes Benchmark + NSA/CISA hardening guide
Pod Security + OPA Gatekeeper / Kyverno for policy
NetworkPolicy default-deny, service mesh for mTLS
Runtime: Falco / Tetragon for threat detection

iq-cloud-05.answer: Time matters — bots scan GitHub continuously. Step 1: immediately rotate the exposed key via IAM — deactivate then delete the access key. Step 2: invalidate any active sessions by changing the user's password and revoking active STS tokens (aws iam delete-access-key, plus a deny-all policy attached to the user as belt-and-braces). Step 3: query CloudTrail for any actions using that access key — IP addresses, regions, services touched, resources affected. If the key was used by anyone other than the developer's own IP, treat as compromise. Step 4: assess blast radius — what permissions did the key have? Run aws iam list-attached-user-policies and simulate-principal-policy. Step 5: remove the secret from git history (BFG Repo-Cleaner or git-filter-repo), force push, and consider the secret permanently burnt regardless — never just delete the commit. Step 6: post-mortem — why did pre-commit hooks not catch this? Deploy gitleaks or trufflehog as a pre-commit hook and as a GitHub Action. Step 7: rotate any downstream secrets the key could have accessed (DB passwords, third-party API keys).
key_points: Speed: bots scan GitHub continuously
Rotate key → revoke sessions → query CloudTrail for use
Clean git history with BFG/filter-repo, never just delete commit
Post-mortem: add gitleaks pre-commit + Action

iq-cloud-06.answer: CSPM — Cloud Security Posture Management — continuously assesses cloud configurations against security benchmarks (CIS, NIST, custom), flagging misconfigurations and drift. It complements IAM Access Analyzer and the cloud provider's native tools by giving multi-cloud coverage and richer prioritisation. Tools I've evaluated or used: Wiz — strong on cloud-native risk graph showing attack paths from internet-exposed asset to crown-jewel data; Prisma Cloud (Palo Alto) — broad coverage including IaC scanning, runtime, and posture; Lacework — anomaly-based detection layered on posture; Orca Security — agentless via side-scanning of cloud disks. Open source options: Prowler — strong AWS coverage, free, easy to run in CI; ScoutSuite; CloudSploit; Steampipe queries for ad-hoc analysis. Selection factors: multi-cloud breadth (AWS-only? add Azure?), IaC scanning to shift-left, attack-path analysis (graph the kill chain, not just list findings), API quality for integration. I'd run Prowler against a single account in 30 minutes to baseline and use the output to make the case for a commercial CSPM.
key_points: CSPM = continuous config assessment against benchmarks
Commercial: Wiz, Prisma, Lacework, Orca
Open source: Prowler, ScoutSuite, CloudSploit, Steampipe
Pick by: multi-cloud, IaC, attack-path analysis

iq-cloud-07.answer: First principle: secrets never land in source code, container images, or environment variables defined at build time. Use a managed secrets store — AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager. Applications fetch secrets at startup or on demand using the workload's identity (IAM role, Kubernetes service account, Vault auth method) — no static credentials carried in the workload. For Kubernetes: External Secrets Operator syncs from Vault/Secrets Manager into Kubernetes Secrets, with namespace scoping. For CI/CD: use OIDC federation so the pipeline authenticates to the cloud without long-lived keys (GitHub Actions → AWS via IAM OIDC provider, no AWS keys in GitHub secrets). Rotation: short-lived dynamic credentials where possible (Vault generates DB users on demand with TTL), automated rotation for long-lived secrets. Monitoring: alert on Secrets Manager API access patterns, alert on unrotated secrets aging beyond policy. Defence in depth: encryption at rest with KMS, audit logging, scope policies to least-privilege secret resource paths.
key_points: Never in code, images, or build-time env vars
Managed store: Secrets Manager / Vault / Key Vault
Workload identity to fetch — no static creds
OIDC federation for CI/CD; short-lived dynamic creds where possible

iq-cloud-08.answer: Container scanning has three pipeline stages: (1) Build-time — scan the image during CI, fail the build on findings above a threshold. I use Trivy or Snyk in CI because they're fast, free for OSS, and catch OS package CVEs plus language dependencies. (2) Registry — schedule daily rescans of pushed images so newly-disclosed CVEs get caught in already-built images. ECR, ACR, and GCR have native scanning; for portability, use Trivy server in the registry pipeline. (3) Runtime — admission controllers (OPA Gatekeeper, Kyverno) block deployment of images with unacceptable risk based on the latest scan; runtime tools (Falco, Tetragon) detect post-deploy compromise. The earlier the better — fixing a CVE in CI is minutes; in production it's hours. Scope of scan: OS packages (apt, apk, yum lockfiles), language packages (pip, npm, gem, go.sum), embedded secrets, misconfigurations (running as root, exposed ports). Trade-off: noisy scans demotivate developers, so I tune severity thresholds and ignore lists carefully with documented rationale.
key_points: Three stages: build, registry, runtime
Trivy and Snyk are my go-to in CI
Daily registry rescans catch new CVEs in old images
Tune thresholds — noisy scans demotivate

iq-cloud-09.answer: Cryptomining alerts usually come from anomalous CPU spike, unusual outbound traffic to mining pools, or EDR/runtime detection of mining binaries. Step 1: identify affected resources — instance IDs, container IDs, regions. Step 2: confirm by looking at process or container metadata — known mining binaries (xmrig, cgminer), connections to known mining pool domains (cross-reference with threat intel feeds for mining IOCs). Step 3: identify the entry point — recent IAM key compromise, exposed credentials in code, vulnerable application exploited, container running with sensitive privileges. Pull CloudTrail and the application logs for the timeframe. Step 4: contain — terminate the compromised resources, revoke credentials, disable user accounts involved. Don't reuse compromised instances. Step 5: estimate cost — cryptomining can run up tens of thousands in compute charges per day; work with finance for credit recovery. Step 6: investigate the root cause and remediate — patch the vulnerable image, rotate IAM keys org-wide if compromise scope is unclear, audit security group changes that exposed the entry point. Step 7: post-mortem and detection improvements.
key_points: Triggers: CPU spike, outbound to mining pools, EDR signature
Confirm with process/container metadata + mining pool IOCs
Identify entry point: credentials, vulnerable app, exposed config
Containment: terminate + rotate; investigate root cause

iq-cloud-10.answer: A VPC is a logically isolated network in the cloud, with private IP space, subnets, route tables, and gateways. Segmentation for security: (1) Multi-AZ subnets — at least three AZs for high availability; each AZ gets a public, private, and database subnet. (2) Public subnets only for internet-facing load balancers and NAT gateways; never for application or database tier. (3) Private application subnets — workloads behind the load balancer, egress to internet via NAT for updates, no direct ingress from internet. (4) Database subnets — completely isolated, no internet routing at all; reachable only from application subnets via security groups. (5) Security groups as stateful firewalls — default deny, explicit allows by source SG ID (not CIDR), enforce least-privilege per workload pair. (6) NACLs as stateless second layer at subnet boundaries for defence-in-depth on sensitive subnets. (7) VPC endpoints for AWS services so traffic to S3 or Secrets Manager doesn't cross the internet. (8) Flow logs to a SIEM. (9) Transit Gateway for hub-spoke between VPCs. (10) Egress filtering via NAT inspection or service like AWS Network Firewall.
key_points: 3-tier subnets per AZ: public / private / database
Database subnets have no internet route
SGs by SG-ID source, not CIDR; default deny
VPC endpoints, flow logs, egress filtering

iq-grc-01.answer: ISO 27001 certification is structured in stages: (1) Gap analysis — assess current state against the standard's controls and management system requirements; identify what exists, what's missing. (2) Scope definition — define what's in and out (which products, locations, infrastructure); narrow scope reduces audit effort but must include critical assets. (3) Risk assessment — identify assets, threats, vulnerabilities, score risks, document treatment. (4) Statement of Applicability — list all Annex A controls, mark applicable or not with justification, document implementation status. (5) Build the ISMS — policies, procedures, documented management commitments, internal audit programme. (6) Implementation period — operate controls for at least 3-6 months so the certifier sees actual evidence, not just documents. (7) Internal audit — verify controls work as documented; capture findings and corrective actions. (8) Management review. (9) Stage 1 external audit — documentation review by the certifier. (10) Stage 2 external audit — on-site / evidence verification. Common failure points: insufficient operating period (no evidence), poor risk treatment documentation, weak internal audit, scope drift.
key_points: Stages: gap → scope → risk → SoA → ISMS → operate → audit
Need 3-6 months operating evidence before Stage 2
Stage 1 doc review, Stage 2 on-site verification
Common fails: insufficient evidence, weak internal audit

How long is certification valid?

iq-grc-02.answer: A risk register is the single source of truth for organisational risks — each entry has a unique ID, risk description, threat source, affected assets, likelihood, impact, inherent risk score, current controls, residual risk score, treatment decision (accept, mitigate, transfer, avoid), owner, due date, status. Keeping it current in a fast-moving engineering org: (1) Tie risk identification to existing engineering ceremonies — risks surfaced in architecture review, post-mortems, security review, threat modelling go straight into the register. (2) Quarterly risk review by the risk committee with mandatory owner attendance — stale risks get re-scored or closed. (3) Connect risk to ticketing — open tickets for treatment actions linked to the risk ID; the risk doesn't close until the ticket does. (4) Automate where possible — pull CSPM findings into a 'tech risk' view of the register; automated risks expire when the finding closes. (5) Make it visible — quarterly snapshot to leadership shows trend lines, not just count. (6) Tie risk acceptance to a documented approver and review date — accepted risks aren't ignored, they're reconfirmed.
key_points: Risk register fields: ID, description, scores, controls, owner, treatment
Capture from architecture reviews, post-mortems, threat models
Quarterly review with owners
Tie to tickets, automate from CSPM, require re-confirmation for accepts
follow_ups: What's the difference between a risk register and a vulnerability tracker?
How do you score likelihood for novel risks?

iq-grc-03.answer: I've used a qualitative 5x5 matrix for most engagements — likelihood and impact each scored 1-5, with definitions for each level documented to drive consistency. Likelihood: 5 = expected within months given current controls; 1 = highly unlikely even over years. Impact: 5 = catastrophic (multi-million loss, regulatory action, brand-defining incident); 1 = negligible. The product gives an inherent risk score; we then subtract control effectiveness to derive residual risk. For quantitative work I've used FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk), which models risk as loss event frequency × loss magnitude with probability distributions instead of single scores. FAIR is rigorous but requires more data and effort — I use it for the top 5-10 risks where the precision matters for board-level investment decisions. Common pitfalls: anchoring on whatever the loudest engineer says (risk-averse engineers inflate, optimists deflate), failing to document scoring rationale, and not updating scores after control changes. I always document the rationale and date the score.
key_points: 5x5 qualitative matrix with documented level definitions
FAIR (quantitative) for top risks driving big investments
Inherent → control effectiveness → residual
Document rationale and date every score
